implementation_notes: scala.concurrent supplies the wait-for-all form: Future.traverse(parts)(f) builds the futures and Future.sequence turns them into a Future[List[T]] that completes when the last partial arrives, all running on the implicit ExecutionContext; the first failure fails the aggregate without cancelling the siblings, so recoverWith or sequencing of Try values handles partial results. Future has no timeout, so a deadline needs a separate scheduled future (or an Akka/Pekko after pattern), while stream libraries (Akka/Pekko Streams, ZIO) are the realizations for push-style aggregation where fold/scan or groupedWithin implements the completeness condition over an actual message stream.
code_sketch:
val aggregate: Future[List[Quote]] =
  Future.traverse(vendors)(v => ask(v))      // completeness: all futures done
val best: Future[Quote] = aggregate.map(_.minBy(_.rate))
Await.result(best, 5.seconds)                 // keep the deadline at the edge
pitfalls: Futures start eagerly on the implicit ExecutionContext: a blocking call inside ask consumes a pool thread and can starve the whole EC; confine blocking with a dedicated pool or blocking{}.
Future.sequence has no timeout: a never-completing partial leaves the aggregate pending forever, which must be handled with an after-timer or a stream/effect library.
Await.result in application code defeats the async model and throws on failure or timeout; aggregate by mapping the Future and keep Await at the system edge.
